The African collared dove (Streptopelia roseogrisea) is a medium-sized columbid native to the Sahelian and Horn of Africa regions, where it inhabits arid savanna and scrubland. Field studies on captive breeding colonies have provided detailed life-history data for this species. Freshly laid eggs weigh approximately 8.3 grams [Ww0 = approximately 8.3 grams], a modest initial investment that reflects the altricial developmental strategy typical of many doves. When eggs are incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], embryonic development proceeds rapidly, and hatching occurs after roughly 13.5 days [ab = roughly 13.5 days]. The newly emerged squab, entirely dependent on crop milk secretion from both parents, has a wet weight at birth of 7 grams [Wwb = 7 grams]. This neonatal mass represents a relatively small fraction of the adult body size, underscoring the pronounced post-hatching growth trajectory that characterizes this species. Comparative data from related congeners suggest that this incubation period and initial mass are consistent with values expected for a bird of this body size and arid-zone adaptation.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods for adult African collared doves, maintained at 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C], the developmental milestones of the nestling phase follow a predictable schedule. The young birds achieve fledging, defined as the age at which they first depart the nest and achieve sustained flight, at 35 days after hatching [tx = 35 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. This relatively protracted nestling period, compared to some smaller columbids, likely reflects the energetic demands of feather development and somatic growth in a species that must rapidly acquire independence in a resource-variable environment. Following fledging, juveniles continue to receive parental provisioning for several additional weeks as they refine foraging skills. The time from hatching to the attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, has been estimated at approximately 105 days after hatching [tp = approximately 105 days after hatching] under these same thermal conditions, indicating that gonadal maturation begins well before the end of the first calendar year at a temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. This relatively early puberty is consistent with a life-history strategy that emphasizes rapid turnover and multiple breeding attempts within a season.

The African collared dove exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism in ultimate adult body mass, a pattern that shapes its reproductive ecology and foraging behavior. Adult females attain a maximum recorded body mass of 148 grams [Wwi = 148 grams], while adult males are substantially larger, reaching a peak adult weight of 165 grams [Wwi = 165 grams]. This approximately 11% difference in body mass between the sexes is relatively modest compared to some other columbid species, but it has implications for parental roles during the breeding cycle. Heavier males are often more successful in territorial defense and courtship displays, whereas the slightly smaller body size of females may facilitate a more efficient allocation of resources toward egg production. These asymptotic masses are attained gradually over the first year of life, following a decelerating growth curve typical of altricial birds. The species' overall body size, intermediate among African doves, positions it within a niche characterized by moderate predation risk and relatively stable food availability from seeds and grains.

Reproductive output in the African collared dove is structured around modest clutch sizes combined with a high annual frequency of nesting attempts, a strategy that maximizes lifetime fecundity in a seasonally unpredictable environment. Females consistently lay 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], a fixed clutch size that is nearly invariant across the genus Streptopelia and that likely represents an energetic optimum balancing egg size against parental provisioning capacity. Complementing this stable per-event output, breeding pairs are capable of raising approximately 4.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 4.5 clutches per year], resulting in a substantial total annual reproductive effort. This high nesting frequency is facilitated by the relatively short nesting cycle and the biparental care system, which allows rapid renesting following successful fledging. The combination of invariant clutch size and prolific multi-brooding is a hallmark of columbid life-history strategy, enabling these birds to exploit ephemeral resource pulses in their arid savanna habitat. First successful breeding typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], a delay of several months beyond the attainment of puberty that may reflect the time required to establish a territory and secure a mate at a temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C].

Longevity records for the African collared dove, gathered from both wild populations and captive maintenance programs, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] under favorable conditions at 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, exceeding that of many smaller passerines, is characteristic of the slower-paced life history observed across the Columbidae and aligns with the species' moderate body size and relatively low annual mortality rate among adults. Wild individuals likely experience shorter average lifespans due to predation, disease, and environmental stochasticity, but the species' capacity for high annual fecundity compensates for this uncertainty. The adult female wet weight of 148 grams [Wwi = 148 grams], achieved during the first year, is sustained throughout the reproductive lifespan, while adult males maintain their larger adult body mass of 165 grams [Wwi = 165 grams] into senescence. These demographic parameters, when integrated, paint a picture of a species with a bet-hedging strategy: early puberty, prolific multi-brooding, and a long potential reproductive window collectively buffer against years of poor breeding success in the variable Sahelian climate.
